newsitem.title: RWANDA: Border stays open as Hutus flood back to Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Border stays open as Hutus flood back to Rwanda.

text.p: Hundreds of trucks crammed with refugees and their meagre belongings were weaving their way across Rwanda on Monday as an estimated 300,000 Hutus returned from a two-year exile in Tanzania.
While many refugees camped overnight along roads from the vast, sprawling camps inside Tanzania, officials kept the border open throughout the night for thousands who kept on walking.

A fleet of trucks, buses and vans was waiting inside Rwanda to give lifts to footsore and weary refugees whose will to remain in Tanzania cracked on Sunday under a brief flurry of blows from stick-wielding Tanzanian soldiers.

The Tanzanians finally lost patience with having to cope with an estimated half a million Hutus who fled Rwanda in fear of reprisal following the genocide of some 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.
"Benaco camp is mostly empty," said an official from the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR. "The next wave will be the refugees that had fled to the northwest and are returning."
That wave of refugees was just around 10 km outside Benaco camp and stretched 90 km (55 miles) to Nyakarura to the north.
Linda Stops, spokeswoman for the International Federation of the Red Cross added: "Benaco is now dying out. The road (to Rwanda from Benaco) was packed. It takes a lot to fill a road."
Refugees crossed into Rwanda overnight but it was not immediately known what percentage of the 300,000 that were forced out of Benaco by Tanzanian troops had entered Rwanda.

Tanzanian soldiers entered the vast Benaco camp, 17 km (10 miles) inside Tanzania, on Sunday and ordered the Rwandans out. Refugees told Reuters that a brief resistance crumbled under a flurry of blows by determined soldiers and the exodus began.

More than one million Hutus -- some connected with the genocide -- reached Zaire and Tanzania in 1994 as the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front routed the former Rwandan army and Iterahamwe militia blamed for the masacres.

More than 600,000 Rwandan Hutus returned home from Zaire last month in an exodus sparked by fighting betwen Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels. Zaire says all the other Rwandan refugees still on its soil must leave as well.
Rwandan radio appealed for truck owners to report to their district offices so the government could hire their vehicles to help to move the refugees.
The private fleet bolstered an effort being co-ordinated by UNHCR to get people home as quickly as possible.

Rwandan and Tanzanian authorities tried to place a news blackout on this operation and journalists in Kigali were barred from the Rusomo crossing on the border, but a Reuters journalist allowed to travel from Benaco to Kigali saw the exodus.

A column of refugees filled the road for many miles. Most walked but some were driving and even pushing the dilapidated vehicles in which they had fled. Some drove cattle and goats they had reared during their exile.
